draft.title: Choosing POS software in Kenya: what to check in a demo
draft.excerpt: Before choosing a POS, try the sale, stock, credit and closing routines your shop needs. Then agree on setup, training, support and the full cost.
draft.markdown:
If your shop is already running, you probably know where the records let you down. Perhaps the stock count never agrees, customer debts live in several notebooks, or you cannot explain the cash left at closing.

Take that problem into the POS demonstration. A useful demo should show you how a normal sale changes the records and how you will check them later. Your staff should also get a turn at the counter.

## Start with a practical demo checklist

Ask the provider to work through these steps using a few items like the ones you sell:

1. Let an operator find the right item, enter a quantity and complete a sale.
2. Try cash, M-Pesa and a split payment. Check the receipt and payment record.
3. Make a credit sale, then record a repayment against an older customer balance.
4. Receive a supplier delivery and check how the stock and supplier balance change.
5. Record damaged stock or a counting correction, including the reason and permissions required.
6. Complete an offline sale and show what happens when the connection returns.
7. Close the till with a cash difference and show what the owner can review.
8. Sign in as a cashier and check which reports, prices and settings they can access.

![Dukarun sale screen with four LED bulbs and two double sockets selected](/assets/workflows/record-sale.webp)

**Example:** Mwangaza Electricals is a fictional shop with one location, an owner and two counter staff. Four 9 W bulbs at KES 250 each and two 13 A double sockets at KES 450 each make a KES 1,900 sale. The item sizes and selling units matter as much as the total. The screenshot uses fictional test data on the actual Dukarun application.

[Request a demo for your shop](/contact?intent=demo&from=/blog/choosing-pos-software-kenya) and tell us which record you want to get right first.

## 1. Does the provider understand your shop?

Explain what you sell, how customers pay, who works at the counter and whether you offer credit. Mention any supplier balances, extra locations or records you need to keep from your current system.

If you sell cable by the coil, ask to see that selling unit. If you sell goods with expiry dates, ask about batches. The demonstration should answer your own working questions.

## 2. Who prepares the starting records?

Agree which products, prices, stock quantities, customer balances and supplier balances will be brought over. Ask what source files are needed, who checks duplicates and who confirms the opening figures.

Be specific about sales history. An old system's export may need preparation, and not every historical record can be transferred. Ask for a test and a way to check the results before you start using the new records.

## 3. Can your staff use it independently?

A cashier should practise a sale, a correction and the closing routine using their own account. The owner should know where to find sales, stock and credit records.

Agree who will attend training, how much practice is included and how a new employee will learn later. Clear guides help, but the useful check is whether your operator can sell and close without someone directing each step.

## 4. What support can you expect?

Ask how to report a problem, when help is available and what is included in the subscription. Confirm how device, printer and unsynchronised-sale problems are handled. Any on-site assistance should be agreed and priced.

Dukarun's team replies to email enquiries within one working day. Setup, training and on-site help can be scoped separately before work begins.

## 5. What happens when the internet drops?

Ask the provider to disconnect during the demo. Complete a sale, find the pending record and reconnect.

Staff need to recognise a sale waiting to synchronise and know how to ask for help if it stays pending. They should also understand the precautions before signing out, clearing the device or moving to another phone. Recording the same sale again can create a new problem.

## 6. How are payments and credit handled?

Check cash, M-Pesa, split payments, credit sales, repayments and refunds. For supplier credit, ask to see a purchase and a later payment against the balance.

Ask exactly how M-Pesa will work with your Till or Paybill. In Dukarun, an active merchant integration can send an STK prompt and confirm payment. A shop can also record a verified M-Pesa receipt where manual confirmation is enabled. Confirm the setup and demonstrate the payment flow you will actually use.

## 7. Will the stock record be useful?

Follow one item from delivery through a sale and a physical count. Ask how damage, returns, transfers and corrections are recorded, and who can make an adjustment.

The software needs clear starting quantities and recorded movements. Your team needs a habit of entering deliveries and sales when they happen. Use the [stock-count checklist](/blog/how-to-track-stock-small-shop-kenya) to prepare.

## 8. What can the owner review?

Ask to see who opened the till, the opening float, recorded payments, closing count and any difference. Check how price changes, refunds and other sensitive actions are linked to an operator or approval.

Separate staff accounts make these records useful. Agree the permissions your cashier, manager and owner need, then try them during the demo. The [owner review checklist](/blog/control-shop-when-you-are-away) gives you a daily routine to test.

## 9. Can you understand and keep your records?

Ask for sales, purchase costs, gross profit, expenses and outstanding balances over the same dates and location. Check the figures with a small example you understand.

Also ask how you can export your records and what happens if you stop using the service. If you need another branch, a public catalogue or customer reminders, confirm what is available and how it is priced.

## 10. What will it cost to start and keep using it?

Get the full scope in writing. It should cover the subscription, users and locations, record preparation, training, payment setup, equipment, travel and any separately charged support or messaging.

[Check Dukarun's current subscription plans](/#pricing), including the price and duration of any introductory access. Introductory access is paid after approval. Implementation is a separate quote when your shop needs it.

A simple shop can begin with a 30-minute orientation, five products and the self-help guides. That starting session does not include a full catalogue migration. Typical assisted implementation engagements exceed KES 40,000, with the price based on the agreed work.

Ask about eTIMS before paying if it is a requirement for your business. Dukarun does not currently submit invoices to eTIMS. Check the provider's current arrangement and the [official KRA eTIMS guidance](https://www.kra.go.ke/online-services/etims).

## Agree what a successful start looks like

Choose someone in the shop to lead the setup. Make time for practice and confirm the starting stock and balances. Before handover, your operator should be able to record a sale and close independently, and you should be able to find the records that address your original problem.

[Read the setup and staff training guide](/blog/dukarun-setup-and-staff-training) or [ask for a setup quote](/contact?intent=setup&from=/blog/choosing-pos-software-kenya). If you are ready to prepare your own records, [create your account](https://app.dukarun.com/register).

draft.title: How to track stock in a small shop in Kenya
draft.excerpt: Keep deliveries, sales and stock corrections in one record. Use this electricals-shop example and count checklist before placing your next order.
draft.markdown:
You are about to order more bulbs. The record says there are 37 left, but someone counts 36 on the shelf. Before buying more, you need to explain that one-piece difference.

A useful stock record keeps track of each delivery, sale and correction. A physical count checks whether those movements agree with what is actually in the shop.

## Follow one product through the day

Our fictional Mwangaza Electricals shop starts with 31 pieces of a 9 W LED bulb. A customer buys four. Later, the shop receives 12 more from a supplier and records two damaged bulbs.

- Opening stock: 31 pieces
- Stock received: 12 pieces
- Bulbs sold: 4 pieces
- Damage recorded: 2 pieces
- Expected stock: 31 + 12 - 4 - 2 = **37 pieces**

The physical count finds 36. Recount first, then check the delivery, sales and damage records. A sale may still be waiting to synchronise, a quantity may have been entered wrongly, or an item may have moved elsewhere. The difference alone does not tell you the cause.

For any product, start with opening stock, add receipts and subtract sales and recorded losses. Include returns, approved corrections and transfers where they apply.

## Keep names and selling units clear

A 9 W bulb and a 12 W bulb need separate records. A fixed 10 m cable coil needs a clear selling unit, just as tape sold by the roll does.

Use the same unit when receiving, selling and counting. Check product names, sizes and pack quantities during setup so staff can choose the right item quickly.

## Record a delivery when it arrives

Check the goods against the supplier's document before putting them away. Record the supplier, product, quantity, location and unit cost. Add batch or expiry details where relevant.

If the supplier will be paid later, record the balance separately. Waiting until the invoice is paid leaves goods on the shelf without a matching stock receipt.

## Record each sale when the item leaves

A daily sales total cannot tell you which bulb or socket was sold. Recording the items and quantities lets you follow the movement later.

![Dukarun sale screen showing bulbs, sockets and available quantities](/assets/workflows/record-sale.webp)

**Sale example:** four bulbs and two sockets are selected in the actual Dukarun application. Completing this sale changes the bulb quantity from 31 to 27 and the socket quantity from 18 to 16. The later delivery and damage in the worked example are separate movements. All screenshot data is fictional.

Dukarun deducts stock when a sale is completed and adds it when a purchase is recorded. If a sale is waiting to synchronise, check its status before entering it again.

## Use this stock-count checklist

1. Choose a quiet period. Pause stock movements or keep them in a separate count-period record.
2. Count one product and location at a time using the recorded selling unit.
3. Separate damaged or expired goods from stock available for sale.
4. Write down the count before looking at the expected quantity.
5. Recount any difference, then check deliveries, sales, returns and transfers.
6. Authorise a correction with a clear reason if the record needs to change.
7. Keep the count date and assign any unresolved difference for follow-up.

Count fast-moving or valuable items more often. A few careful checks each week can find a problem before the next full shop count.

Dukarun records adjustment reasons, with access controlled by permissions. Batches can retain purchase costs and expiry details, and transfers record movement between locations. [Read the inventory guide](/docs#inventory) for the available controls.

## Use the record to decide when to order

A simple reorder estimate is:

**Average daily sales × supplier delivery days + safety stock.**

If a product sells five pieces a day, delivery takes three days and you keep five spare pieces, the estimate is 20 pieces. Place the order around that level, then adjust for demand, delivery reliability, available cash and shelf space. Check expiry risk where it applies.

You can make a better buying decision when the quantity is supported by recent movements and a count.

[Request a sale-to-stock demo](/contact?intent=demo&from=/blog/how-to-track-stock-small-shop-kenya). Ask us to follow one item from delivery through a sale and a count. For the money side of the same routine, read [how to reconcile cash and M-Pesa](/blog/how-to-reconcile-cash-mpesa-shop).

draft.title: How to know your shop profit: a worked example in KES
draft.excerpt: A busy day can still leave you unsure what the shop earned. Separate sales, purchase costs, expenses and customer repayments with this worked example.
draft.markdown:
The shop was busy, customers paid by cash and M-Pesa, and a few bought on credit. How much did the business earn?

Start with the value sold, subtract the cost of those items, then subtract the costs of running the shop. The money in the drawer needs a separate check.

## Know which number you are looking at

- **Sales:** the full value of goods or services sold, including credit sales.
- **Cost of goods sold:** what the shop paid for the items sold. Stock still on the shelf is not included in this day's cost of sales.
- **Gross profit:** sales minus the cost of goods sold.
- **Operating expenses:** costs such as wages, delivery, rent, electricity and business airtime.
- **Profit in this example:** gross profit minus the day's operating expenses.

This is a simplified daily example. Formal accounts may also need taxes, other adjustments and costs allocated over a longer period.

## Work through one trading day

The fictional Mwangaza Electricals shop records:

- Cash sales: KES 8,400
- M-Pesa sales: KES 6,300
- Credit sales: KES 1,500
- **Total sales: KES 16,200**

The goods sold cost the shop KES 11,000. Gross profit is therefore **KES 5,200**.

The day's operating expenses are KES 1,200 in wages, KES 500 for delivery and KES 200 for business airtime, making KES 1,900 in total.

**KES 5,200 gross profit - KES 1,900 expenses = KES 3,300 profit.**

These are illustrative daily totals, separate from the single KES 1,900 sale in the website counter demo.

## Keep customer repayments separate

The KES 1,500 credit sale contributes to today's sales, but the customer has not paid it yet.

Now suppose customers repay KES 1,000 from older purchases: KES 600 in cash and KES 400 by M-Pesa. That money reduces their outstanding balances. Counting it as a new sale would record the same income twice.

For this day:

- Today's cash and M-Pesa sales bring in KES 14,700.
- Older customer debts bring in another KES 1,000.
- **Total receipts are KES 15,700.**

The shop has KES 16,200 in sales, KES 15,700 in receipts and KES 3,300 in profit. Each figure answers a different question.

![Dukarun customer account showing Amina Hassan's KES 1,500 outstanding balance](/assets/workflows/customer-credit.webp)

**Credit example:** fictional electrician customer Amina Hassan owes KES 1,500 from an earlier purchase. This screenshot shows a separate example account, not the new credit sale in the daily totals above. Check the balance before recording a repayment. The names and amounts are fictional test data on the actual Dukarun application.

## Check the drawer at closing

The shop opened with KES 2,000 in cash. Of the KES 1,900 operating expenses, KES 500 was paid from the drawer and KES 1,400 from another business account. A further KES 4,000 was removed for banking.

Expected cash is:

**KES 2,000 opening float + KES 8,400 cash sales + KES 600 repayments - KES 500 payouts - KES 4,000 banked = KES 6,500.**

Expected M-Pesa receipts are **KES 6,300 + KES 400 = KES 6,700**.

If the drawer contains KES 6,400, investigate the KES 100 shortage. Recount and check payment methods, repayments, payouts and cash removals. The KES 6,500 expected cash and KES 3,300 profit are still separate figures.

[Use the free cash-up tool](/tools/daily-shop-cash-up) to compare your records with counted cash and confirmed M-Pesa receipts. No account is needed, and the figures stay in the open page's memory.

## Check costs before trusting the profit figure

Keep purchase costs current and use the same date range and location when comparing reports. Do not subtract a supplier payment as another cost if the cost of those sold goods is already included. The payment settles a balance; check the purchase and payment records together.

In Dukarun, a completed sale connects the payment method, stock movement, revenue, cost of goods sold and gross margin. [Read the reporting guide](https://dukarun.gitbook.io/docs/money-and-reporting/understanding-the-financial-result) and check a small example against your own records.

[Request a demo of sales, credit and closing](/contact?intent=demo&from=/blog/how-to-know-shop-profit-kenya). If the money check is your main concern, start with the [cash and M-Pesa reconciliation guide](/blog/how-to-reconcile-cash-mpesa-shop).

draft.title: How to keep track of your shop when you are away
draft.excerpt: Use individual staff accounts, cashier sessions and a short daily review to understand sales, stock changes and closing differences while you are away.
draft.markdown:
When you leave the shop with your staff, you still need to know what sold, what changed and whether the money agrees at closing.

A few clear routines make that review easier: each person uses their own account, sales belong to a cashier session, and sensitive changes keep a reason or approval. You can then ask about a specific record instead of trying to reconstruct the whole day.

## Give each operator their own account

A shared login makes it difficult to tell who handled a sale or changed a record. Give cashiers the access they need to serve customers, and keep reporting, settings and approvals with the people responsible for them.

Try the roles during setup. Sign in as a cashier and check what they can see and change. Then sign in as the owner and find the records you expect to review.

## Start and finish with a cashier session

A session connects the opening float, the operator's sales and the closing count. It should tell you:

- Who opened the till and where they were working.
- How much cash was counted at opening.
- Which sales and payments were recorded.
- How much cash was expected and counted at closing.
- What difference remains to be explained.

Keep receipts linked to the completed sale so a later question has a clear reference. Any refund or reversal should remain connected to the original transaction.

## Agree which actions need approval

Choose controls that fit the shop's work. A refund, reversal, price change or credit decision may need a manager's permission. An ordinary sale should remain straightforward for the cashier.

Ask to see how an approval is requested, who can decide and where the decision is recorded. The available actions depend on the permissions and setup you choose.

## Review a closing difference calmly

At fictional Mwangaza Electricals, owner Njeri reviews Wanjiru's session:

- Opening cash: KES 2,000
- Cash sales: KES 8,400
- Cash repayments of older debts: KES 600
- Recorded cash payout: KES 500
- Cash removed for banking: KES 4,000
- **Expected closing cash: KES 6,500**
- Counted cash: KES 6,400
- **Difference: KES 100 short**

![Dukarun closing review showing KES 6,500 expected cash and KES 6,400 counted](/assets/workflows/check-closing.webp)

**Closing example:** the actual Dukarun screen shows Wanjiru's declaration against the expected amount. This is a fictional trading day, separate from the single sale in the website counter demo.

Start by recounting and reviewing the payout, banking removal, repayments and payment methods. A difference needs an explanation, but the figure alone does not prove what happened.

For a manual record, the [free daily cash-up tool](/tools/daily-shop-cash-up) gives you the same starting check.

## Follow up stock changes too

If the shop starts with 18 double sockets and sells two, the expected quantity is 16. A count of 15 leaves one socket to explain.

Check sales, deliveries, damage, transfers and adjustments. If a correction is needed, keep the reason and the person who authorised it. The [stock-count checklist](/blog/how-to-track-stock-small-shop-kenya) gives staff a repeatable process.

Dukarun's audit history records important actions so you can review who did what and when. Use it to investigate a specific sale, correction or approval alongside the related business record.

## Keep the daily owner review short

1. Confirm the operator, location and session you are reviewing.
2. Compare the opening float, recorded cash movements and closing count.
3. Compare M-Pesa receipts with the merchant record for the same period.
4. Review new credit sales and older debt repayments separately.
5. Check sensitive changes and their reasons or approvals.
6. Confirm pending offline sales have synchronised before relying on the full day's totals.
7. Assign any unresolved difference to someone, with a date to follow up.

Ask the operator to explain a difference while the day is still fresh. Clear records make that conversation fairer and more useful for both of you.

Dukarun connects staff roles, cashier sessions, receipts, approvals and audit history. [Read about cashier sessions](/docs#cashier-sessions) and [team permissions](/docs#approvals), then [request a cashier-and-owner demo](/contact?intent=demo&from=/blog/control-shop-when-you-are-away).

Use the [cash reconciliation guide](/blog/how-to-reconcile-cash-mpesa-shop) for the daily money check. During [setup and training](/blog/dukarun-setup-and-staff-training), agree who will do each part of the routine.

draft.title: Recording salon sales with a barcode service menu
draft.excerpt: Use the Android phones your salon team already has to record services and payments. Start with a few services, then add a barcode menu if it helps.
draft.markdown:
When a customer finishes a treatment, staff need a quick way to record the service and payment. A short barcode menu can help them select the right service from a phone and keep the sale linked to their account.

This example suits a small salon with Android phones already in use. Start with one or two common services and try the routine with your team before preparing the full menu.

## Set up the services and staff accounts

Create each treatment as a service without inventory tracking. Give it a clear name, a base price and a unique barcode. Each employee should use their own Dukarun account, with permissions that fit their work.

![A salon service configured in Dukarun without inventory tracking](https://supa.dukarun.com/storage/v1/object/public/blog-media/8b739c39-a7c8-4e78-a275-ff415485846d/90d9b79b-e402-4c62-ad0c-0f9e0d3b5b04.svg)

Agree who can change prices. If the final charge depends on the treatment, authorised staff should record the actual price and reason.

## Try the phones before buying equipment

Employees can search for a service by name, so you can practise without a label printer. If scanning makes the work easier, choose a label printer supported by the phone's normal Android print service.

Check that it can print your intended labels, such as 50 × 30 mm adhesive labels, at 100% scale without unwanted margins or headers. Test one label on the actual device before buying or printing a full set.

Dukarun uses the device's normal print dialog. A Bluetooth connection alone does not confirm printer compatibility. Use the [hardware checklist](/docs/hardware) and ask for a current equipment quote.

## Prepare a small barcode menu

Open **Products → Print labels**, generate any missing barcodes and print a label for each common service.

![Barcode labels being generated for salon services](https://supa.dukarun.com/storage/v1/object/public/blog-media/8b739c39-a7c8-4e78-a275-ff415485846d/c81b9e09-6606-4506-af09-654229f216f8.svg)

Put the labels on a clean, laminated menu near the workstation or payment counter. Staff can scan from this sheet when recording a sale. It can be kept for staff use.

## Record the service and payment

1. Sign in on the phone and open **POS → Sell**.
2. Search for the service or tap **Scan** and use the barcode menu.
3. Add any other services provided.
4. Have an authorised employee confirm a price change where needed.
5. Select cash, M-Pesa or a split payment and complete the sale.
6. Provide a receipt using the agreed method.

![A phone sale example alongside the cashier closing screen](https://supa.dukarun.com/storage/v1/object/public/blog-media/8b739c39-a7c8-4e78-a275-ff415485846d/696e2244-0aa1-4b91-b277-9076e1fe63e8.svg)

Using individual accounts identifies who recorded each sale. If a receptionist takes all payments, agree how the employee who provided the service will be identified. Recording the payment and crediting the service provider are separate responsibilities to check during setup.

## Close and review the day

At closing, the cashier counts the drawer and closes their session. Dukarun compares counted and expected cash and records the difference.

The owner can review completed sales and staff activity from the day's records. M-Pesa receipts should also be checked against the merchant record for the same period. Follow the [cash and M-Pesa guide](/blog/how-to-reconcile-cash-mpesa-shop) if you need a closing checklist.

## Keep the routine suited to your salon

For fixed prices, staff can select the service and charge. For variable prices, keep a sensible base price and restrict adjustments to authorised employees. A shared front desk may work better than each employee taking payments.

This guide covers service sales, payments, receipts and cashier records. Dukarun does not provide appointment scheduling or salon-specific treatment records, so keep an agreed process for those needs.

[Request a salon sales demo](/contact?intent=demo&from=/blog/salon-sales-with-barcode-service-menu) using a few of your common services. [Check current subscription plans](/#pricing) and read the [setup and staff training guide](/blog/dukarun-setup-and-staff-training) if you need help preparing records or training the team. That assistance is quoted separately.

If you are ready to configure the services yourself, [create your account](https://app.dukarun.com/register). Access requires approval and payment under the current offer.

draft.title: Building Dukarun V2: what Kenyan shops taught us
draft.excerpt: Customer credit, supplier balances, unreliable internet and busy counters shaped Dukarun V2. Here is why we brought these daily records together.
draft.markdown:
A shop owner should be able to find out what sold, what remains on the shelf, who owes money and whether the day made a profit.

For many businesses, those answers are spread across notebooks, supplier documents, M-Pesa records and the last stock count. As more staff and products join the shop, keeping them in step takes more work.

We started Dukarun to bring those records together. The first version focused on sales and stock. Working with Kenyan businesses showed us how much else a sale can affect.

## The questions that shaped the product

Customer credit was part of ordinary trading. Owners needed to see what a trusted customer still owed and record a later repayment correctly.

Supplier credit mattered too. Goods could arrive before an invoice was paid, so stock and supplier balances needed to stay connected.

Internet interruptions happened during working hours. A cashier needed to keep serving customers and know which sales were waiting to synchronise.

Owners also needed different access for different staff. Cashiers needed a quick counter routine, managers needed approvals and owners needed records they could review.

These working questions shaped the features we added and the decision to rebuild the foundation for V2.

## What happens behind a sale

Consider the fictional Mwangaza Electricals demo: four bulbs and two sockets make a KES 1,900 sale. The cashier chooses the items, records the payment and completes it.

The records then need to agree on the quantities sold, stock remaining, money received, purchase costs and cashier responsible. If the sale is on credit, the customer balance needs to change as well.

![Dukarun counter with four bulbs and two sockets selected for a KES 1,900 sale](/assets/workflows/record-sale.webp)

**Demo example:** Mwangaza Electricals, its staff, prices and quantities are fictional. The screenshot uses the actual Dukarun application with test data.

Offline sales add another step. The sale is kept on the device, synchronised when the connection returns and recorded once. The cashier needs a clear pending status while that happens.

[Try the electricals counter example](/#how-it-works) or use the [demo checklist](/blog/choosing-pos-software-kenya) to choose the routines you want to see.

## Rebuilding around connected records

As the earlier product grew, maintaining the connections between sales, payments, stock and balances became harder. V2 gave us a chance to build those relationships into a stronger foundation.

Moving records from V1 also required care. A product list on its own does not preserve the payments, purchases and customer balances behind it. Migration work included checks on those linked records.

For a shop moving from another system today, the same lesson applies: agree which records will move and how you will confirm them before starting daily use.

## What the daily routines cover

**At the counter:** staff can find products through search, quick selections, a device camera or compatible barcode hardware. Sales support cash, M-Pesa, split payments and customer credit, with offline selling and later synchronisation.

**For stock and suppliers:** completed sales deduct stock, while recorded purchases add it and keep supplier balances. Stock adjustments, batches, expiry details and transfers support the relevant shop routines.

**For customer credit:** balances, limits, payment history and statements help staff review an account before extending more credit or recording a repayment. Customer documents can be sent manually through SMS or WhatsApp, and payment reminders can be configured.

**At closing:** cashier sessions connect opening float, recorded activity, expected cash and the counted amount. Roles, approvals and audit history help the owner follow up important changes.

**In the books:** sales, purchases, expenses and balances feed into double-entry records and reports. The owner can trace a figure back to the transactions behind it.

**Online:** a public product catalogue lets customers browse and enquire through WhatsApp.

Confirm the features, permissions and payment setup you need during a demo. Merchant M-Pesa integration must be configured and active before relying on its payment prompts.

## Start with the routine your shop needs most

You may need trustworthy stock quantities, clearer customer balances or a closing check you can explain. Start there, with a few products and an operator who can practise.

Our early customers helped us understand these priorities through their daily use and support questions. We are grateful for that work and continue to use it when improving Dukarun.

[Request a demo for your shop](/contact?intent=demo&from=/blog/building-dukarun-v2-pos-software-kenya). Tell us which record you want to improve. [Check current subscription plans](/#pricing) and the [setup and training guide](/blog/dukarun-setup-and-staff-training) before deciding how to start. Introductory access is paid after approval, and assisted implementation is quoted separately when needed.

If you are ready to prepare your own shop, [create your account](https://app.dukarun.com/register) and follow the [product guides](/docs).

draft.title: Dukarun setup and staff training: getting your shop ready
draft.excerpt: Prepare products, stock, balances and staff before starting. Choose self-start or quoted assistance, then check that your operator can sell and close independently.
draft.markdown:
Before the first day on a new POS, someone needs to confirm the starting records and someone needs to practise the counter routine. In a small shop, the owner can often lead both.

A useful handover ends with your operator able to record a sale and close without being talked through each step. Agree on that outcome before arranging training.

## Begin with a few familiar products

Start with one location, the owner or an operator, and five products you sell regularly. Use clear names, sizes, selling units, prices and purchase costs.

Our fictional Mwangaza Electricals shop starts with a 9 W bulb, a 13 A double socket, a 20 A circuit breaker, a fixed 10 m cable coil and an insulation tape roll. These make useful practice items because the team can recognise them and check their units.

A simple shop can begin with a 30-minute orientation and the self-help guides. That session introduces the sale and closing routine. Preparing a full catalogue and checking historical balances may take more work.

## Prepare the records you will start with

- **Products or services:** names, sizes, selling units, prices and barcodes where used. Resolve duplicates and unclear pack sizes.
- **Opening stock:** counted quantities for each product and location, with a count date.
- **Purchase costs:** use the records you have and identify missing costs for follow-up.
- **Customer and supplier balances:** names, contacts and evidence of the amounts still owed.
- **Opening cash and payment methods:** agree the float and how cash and M-Pesa will be recorded.
- **Staff:** names, individual accounts and the tasks each person should be allowed to perform.
- **Devices:** a working phone or computer, internet access for setup and synchronisation, and any printer you plan to use.

The owner should confirm stock and balances. Someone else can organise a spreadsheet, but they need your agreement on what the shop actually owns and owes.

If you are changing systems, agree which history can be brought over and which source files are needed. Keep time for checking the result before using it at the counter.

## Choose how much help you need

**Self-start** suits an owner who can prepare the records, follow the guides and practise with staff. [Create your account](https://app.dukarun.com/register), check the approval and paid access requirements, and use the [product documentation](/docs).

**Assisted implementation** suits a shop that needs help organising data, confirming opening records or training several employees. The subscription and that work are priced separately. [Check current subscription plans](/#pricing). Typical implementation engagements exceed KES 40,000, with the scope and price agreed before work begins.

## Make the setup quote specific

Ask the quote to state:

- Which products, balances, locations and source files are included.
- Who cleans the data and who confirms the opening records.
- Which staff will attend and how many training sessions are included.
- What is covered for payment configuration, device checks, travel and equipment.
- How errors found during checking will be resolved.
- What support follows handover and what needs another quote.
- The completion criteria, payment arrangements and any unfinished work.

If you need custom features, more historical records or extra training, put them in the scope before work starts. The owner remains responsible for supplying and confirming the business information.

## Let the operator practise

![Dukarun sale screen with four bulbs and two sockets selected](/assets/workflows/record-sale.webp)

**Training example:** Wanjiru selects four bulbs and two sockets for a KES 1,900 sale at fictional Mwangaza Electricals. The screenshot uses the actual application with test data.

Ask your operator to repeat a sale using the right item, unit and payment method. Then find the remaining stock. Add a customer repayment and stock receipt if those are part of your normal work.

Practise closing too. Show where the opening float, payouts and cash removals are recorded, and how to follow up a difference. Staff should use their own role, recognise pending offline sales and know where to ask for help.

## Check that the shop can work independently

Before handover, check that:

1. The operator records a sale with the correct items and payment method independently.
2. The operator completes the closing routine and can explain where a difference needs checking.
3. The owner finds the sales, stock or credit record that addresses the shop's original problem.
4. Opening stock and balances have been checked and approved.
5. Staff know where the guides are and how to contact support.
6. Any unfinished task has an owner and due date, with its effect on handover agreed.

[Request a setup quote](/contact?intent=setup&from=/blog/dukarun-setup-and-staff-training) and tell us about your current records and the help you need. If you are still choosing a POS, start with the [demo checklist](/blog/choosing-pos-software-kenya). For closing practice, use the [cash and M-Pesa guide](/blog/how-to-reconcile-cash-mpesa-shop).

draft.title: How to reconcile cash and M-Pesa in your shop
draft.excerpt: Work out what should be in the drawer and which M-Pesa receipts should have arrived. Follow a simple closing example with sales, repayments and payouts.
draft.markdown:
At closing, you need to answer two questions: does the cash in the drawer agree with the records, and do the M-Pesa receipts agree for the same period?

Work out the expected amounts first. Then count or confirm what actually arrived. If there is a difference, check the records before deciding why.

## Separate today's sales from older debt repayments

A cash sale brings money into the drawer. A new credit sale increases the customer's balance but brings no money in yet. When a customer repays an older debt, record it against that balance and the payment method used.

Cash repayments affect the drawer; M-Pesa repayments affect M-Pesa receipts. Counting an old repayment as another sale would inflate today's sales. The [shop profit example](/blog/how-to-know-shop-profit-kenya) explains how these totals fit together.

## Work out the expected cash

On a fictional trading day at Mwangaza Electricals:

- Opening float is KES 2,000.
- Cash sales are KES 8,400.
- Customers repay KES 600 of older debts in cash.
- Recorded cash payouts are KES 500.
- KES 4,000 is removed for banking.

**Expected cash = KES 2,000 + KES 8,400 + KES 600 - KES 500 - KES 4,000 = KES 6,500.**

The shop also makes KES 1,500 in new credit sales. That amount contributes to sales but adds no cash to this closing calculation.

If the drawer contains KES 6,400, it is KES 100 short. Recount, then check the opening float, payment choices, repayments, payouts and banking removal.

Keep a reason and destination for cash removed from the drawer. Moving money to a business bank account changes where it is held; it does not make it an operating expense.

## Check M-Pesa receipts for the same period

The same example day has KES 6,300 in M-Pesa sales and KES 400 in M-Pesa repayments of older debts.

**Expected M-Pesa receipts = KES 6,300 + KES 400 = KES 6,700.**

If confirmed receipts for that merchant account and period are KES 6,700, the receipts agree. The KES 100 cash shortage still needs its own review.

Use incoming receipts for this comparison. The closing M-Pesa balance can also change through withdrawals, transfers, fees and payments out. A balance alone cannot show whether the recorded customer receipts arrived.

## Use the free cash-up tool

1. Enter cash, M-Pesa and credit sales for the period.
2. Add older debt repayments under the payment method used.
3. Enter the opening float, cash payouts and removals.
4. Count closing cash and confirm M-Pesa receipts for the same period.
5. Review each difference against the source records.

[Open the daily shop cash-up tool](/tools/daily-shop-cash-up). No account is needed. Your figures stay in the open page's memory and are not added to its demo invitation.

The tool compares figures you enter; it does not fetch an M-Pesa statement or reconcile the whole wallet. A blank count shows “Not checked”. Printing the summary gives you a review copy, rather than entering it into Dukarun's business records.

## Follow up a difference

- Check that the dates, location and merchant account match.
- Recount cash and confirm the opening float.
- Review cash versus M-Pesa choices, split payments and refunds.
- Match each repayment to the customer balance and payment method.
- Check payouts and removals against their notes.
- Confirm pending offline sales have synchronised.
- Record any unresolved amount, who will investigate and when.

![Dukarun closing screen showing KES 6,500 expected cash and KES 6,400 counted](/assets/workflows/check-closing.webp)

**Closing example:** Wanjiru's declaration is KES 100 below the expected amount. The actual application screen uses fictional test data for this separate trading day. It is not the closing result of the single sale in the website counter demo.

## Make it a routine the team can repeat

Give each operator their own account and agree who reviews differences. The [daily owner checklist](/blog/control-shop-when-you-are-away) helps keep that review short.

[Request a demo of sales and closing](/contact?intent=demo&from=/blog/how-to-reconcile-cash-mpesa-shop). If you want help preparing the records or training staff, read the [setup guide](/blog/dukarun-setup-and-staff-training) before asking for a separately scoped quote.
